core_insight: SOLID is not about clean code, it is about containing the impact of change by isolating reasons to change and depending on abstractions.

scenes.voice: You ship a service. Six months later a new payment provider is requested. The change touches five classes, tests break elsewhere, and a teammate's PR conflicts. Why does a small request become risky?
scenes.visual: Simple timeline graphic: Ship → 6 months → New requirement → Red arrows spreading to 5 classes, tests, PR conflict.

scenes.voice: The problem is not bad developers. It is change coupling. Responsibilities pile up in the same units, behaviors leak across boundaries, and abstractions get reused in ways they were never designed for.
scenes.visual: City plan metaphor: one neighborhood labeled with multiple purposes, roads tangled.

scenes.voice: The obvious approach is to just edit the existing class. Add an if for the new provider, tweak the discount, add a notification call. It works today.
scenes.visual: Code box with OrderService creating Stripe client directly, applying discount, sending email, logging all in one.

scenes.voice: Constraint: every new requirement forces you to open the same core file. That couples payment, pricing, and notification. A change to logging can break billing. Tests in unrelated modules fail.
scenes.visual: Same class box with arrows labeled payment, pricing, notification, logging all pointing in.
scenes.on_screen_text: One class, many reasons to change

scenes.voice: SOLID is a set of design contracts to make change cheaper. Single Responsibility: one reason to change per class. Open/Closed: extend behavior without editing existing code. Depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.
scenes.visual: Mermaid diagram showing Checkout Policy depending on PaymentPort abstraction with StripeAdapter, AdyenAdapter, FakePayment implementing it.
scenes.mermaid:
graph TD
    A[Checkout Policy] --> I[PaymentPort]
    B[StripeAdapter] --> I
    C[AdyenAdapter] --> I
    D[FakePayment] --> I
    A -.depends on abstraction.-> I
    B -.implements.-> I

scenes.voice: Now a new provider is a new adapter implementing PaymentPort. Checkout policy stays closed for modification. Tests inject FakePayment with no network. High-level policy is stable while implementations vary.
scenes.visual: Before/after split: Before = OrderService with direct Stripe; After = OrderService with ports PaymentPort, PricingPolicy, NotificationPort.
scenes.on_screen_text: New class, not a diff in core

scenes.voice: Trade-off: you pay indirection and more files. Over-modularization creates navigation tax. If there is only one implementation and no test need, the abstraction adds cost. Use SOLID when change is the primary risk, skip ceremonial abstraction for throwaway code.
scenes.visual: Scale graphic: Change cost down, complexity up.

scenes.voice: Mental model: think of a codebase as a city plan. One neighborhood for one purpose. Change one street without rebuilding the city.
scenes.visual: City map with clearly separated neighborhoods: Payments, Pricing, Notifications.

mental_model: A codebase is a city plan. Each class is a neighborhood with one purpose. Isolate reasons to change so a change in one neighborhood does not force rebuilding others. Depend on abstractions so high-level policy stays stable while implementations vary.
final_takeaway: SOLID is about containing change, not aesthetics. Isolate reasons to change and depend on abstractions.
